title: How Sainz’s home race in Madrid unravelled
excerpt:
If there was one weekend this year where Carlos Sainz was hoping that better Williams form and perhaps some attrition ahead would combine to propel him up the order it was always going to be his home race in Madrid.

Unfortunately, while the local hero received huge support, the new track did not favour the Williams FW48 from the start of practice on the car’s final outing before the Baku upgrade package arrives.

Things began to fall apart for Sainz in Qualifying, and then a first lap incident scuppered any chance of making progress. And it didn’t go much better for his Williams team mate Alex Albon.

The pair qualified in P16 and P17, with Albon ahead, and the fact that they were split by just 0.005s in Q1 suggested that both men had found the limit of the car.

It then got worse for Sainz as he received a three-place grid penalty for impeding Valtteri Bottas that sent him down to P20, behind the two Cadillacs.

Wary of how hard overtaking was expected to be, Sainz went for it at the start and he paid the price when he made contact with the Racing Bulls of Yuki Tsunoda at Turn 1, picking up some floor damage in the process.

"I had a really good start off the line,” he said. “I think I got three or four positions on the hard tyre, and then a lot of bunching up into Turn 1 caught me a bit out, and I had a small contact with Tsunoda that damaged my floor.

“Unfortunately from there on, I had damage in the car, and it was a race of survival, because I had no rear downforce in the car for the rest of the race.

“So yeah, we had nothing to lose on that Lap 1, and I wanted to get a good start to see if we could get anything going in this race.”

A little later Sainz got into another scrape at Turn 5, this time with his countryman Fernando Alonso, who felt he was squeezed.

Having damaged his front wing Alonso made his feelings about the incident clear on team radio, and just for good measure he reminded the world – and the stewards – of Sainz’s first corner mishap.

“Nothing to say really,” Sainz noted. “It's the nature of that corner when you turn right, and I think he complained on the radio, so he managed to get me a penalty, like always. I think it's the nature of that corner, it's always going to lead to these kinds of crashes, because there's only space for one.

“There's not even space for two. So yeah, and you cannot keep looking in your mirror while you're turning, and doing a right/left because you need to look forward. So at one point you need to focus on your own driving line, and I don't think Fernando was alongside me or anything.”

Sainz took a five-second penalty at his pit stop. Given the floor damage and the impact on performance the team eventually decided that it wasn’t worth continuing, and the car was retired after 43 laps.

“Just there was no downforce in the car,” he said. “So I was just driving around one second off the pace with the floor damage. It was slight damage, honestly, it wasn't that big of a contact, but with these cars, the moment you lose a piece of the floor, it's game over.”

He added: “But in reality, even with a perfect race, we wouldn't have finished higher than 16th. So yeah, not a lot to fight for today.”

It was not what Sainz wanted for his home town race, but on the plus side he at least enjoyed the love that he received from the crowd.

“Honestly, it was an amazing weekend on that front,” he said. “I truly enjoyed seeing the support that we got from all the fans. Their behaviour, the support that I've caught this weekend is second to none, and I cannot thank them enough for making me feel so at home in my home.

“And I’m looking forward already to next year. As I said in many interviews, hopefully this is the last year here in Madrid that I'm fighting for P16, and from next year onwards I can fight for something more, because honestly, it's not ideal to be fighting at home for a P15, P16 all weekend.”

Meanwhile it was an equally frustrating Sunday in Madrid for Albon, who ended up in the better of those two positions. However he struggled for pace throughout, coming under pressure from Cadillac’s Sergio Perez.

“I think one of my stronger weekends, but at the same time, just super, super sketchy,” said Albon. “Realistically, the pace isn't quick enough, and I think, especially on the harder tyres, we don't have the load to keep the tyre alive. So that tyre has actually got very little degradation, but it just cools down once the tread comes off the tyre.

“You need to keep pushing on it to keep the temps up. We don't have the grip to do it. Just the tyres get cold, basically.”

title: Tsunoda reviews Madrid outing after sustaining 'big damage'
excerpt:
Yuki Tsunoda endured a race to forget in Madrid, as the Racing Bulls stand-in finished down in 14th on a day that could end up being his final Formula 1 start.

After being hit by Carlos Sainz at the first corner, he was left driving a damaged Racing Bulls car and thus never had a chance to make any progress.

The Madring was Tsunoda’s third outing as replacement for Liam Lawson, who in turn was drafted into Red Bull to deputise for the injured Isack Hadjar.

Tsunoda put himself back on the F1 radar with a solid P11 in the Dutch GP, and by subsequently scoring a point with P10 at Monza.

Another good run in Madrid would have further strengthened his case to return to a race seat in the future and it looked good on Friday when he finished FP2 in eighth, his team mate Arvid Lindblad having demonstrated the potential of the VCARB 03 with P4 before his big crash.

However, when it mattered in Qualifying on Saturday things drifted away from Tsunoda and he could qualify only P15.

“Yesterday, I knew there are a lot of places I can improve, from the car and everything,” he said after the session. “Something didn't really click today. Just pace was not there at all.

“Somehow, just it degs a little bit in terms of car pace. I just didn't feel any tyre grip, even sometimes it felt old tyres were better than new tyres. Something felt very odd, so I have to find out why. In general, I just didn't have grip.”

That misfortune continued into Tsunoda’s race day, which was compromised from the start when he was hit hard on the left side by Sainz.

Not only did he lose spots to Alex Albon and Sergio Perez, but he also sustained damage that made it even harder for him to find a way past the Cadillac driver.

“Pretty much the race was finished by that,” he said after the flag. “I lost a lot of positions by that, but also I had a big damage from that. Honestly, it was very difficult to overtake here, even though I had a still good advantage to the car in front in terms of pace. But just a really pressurising race, honestly.”

While the Racing Bulls had the potential to be faster than Perez, there was nothing that Tsunoda could do. However, when Perez pitted under the VSC, Tsunoda was able to find some performance.

“I mean, suddenly the car got cleared in front, and the pace suddenly recovered a lot. And to be honest, considering that damage I had, the pace wasn't that bad. But yeah, it was super difficult to overtake here.”

At the chequered flag he was in P14, which was not what he wanted on a day when Lindblad finished P9.

“In general there's something this week that wasn't easy at all,” he said. “And being unable to, I would say, solve the issue that I had since FP1, probably for me that issue got worse and worse throughout the week. So yeah, something to review. I mean, in the race, nothing I can do.”

title: Mekies assesses Lawson's Red Bull stint after Madrid
excerpt:
Laurent Mekies has praised Liam Lawson's "very strong" stint with Red Bull, with the New Zealander standing in for the injured Isack Hadjar across the last three race weekends.

Lawson's promotion back to Red Bull, albeit on a temporary basis, has been a chance of redemption after the 24-year-old managed just two race weekends for the team at the start of the 2025 season before being sent back to Racing Bulls.

His latest stint with the senior squad has been much more positive with seventh on his first outing in Zandvoort, while he backed that up with a solid sixth last weekend in Madrid.

With plenty more experience under his belt, Red Bull team boss Mekies has been impressed with what Lawson has managed to achieve so far.

“I think he's done a very good job," he said. "I think we all know how difficult it is to jump to a different team, to a different car, and I think that he has done that to the best of what could have been our expectations.

“He has taken some very important points today with the P6. He did the same in Zandvoort and in Monza he would have done something similar without the contact with Nico [Hulkenberg] and the front wing damage.

“So, I think he did a very good job, again very different pictures compared to the first two races of 2025 when he was in the team so we are thankful and happy with that.”

During his brief stint with Red Bull at the start of 2025, Lawson qualified 18th and 20th in his two qualifying sessions with the team and he was also 20th on the grid for the first Sprint of the season. He failed to score in either Australia or China, in stark contrast to team mate Max Verstappen who finished those races second and fourth.

But thus far, his second Red Bull stint has been much more positive. He has qualified eighth twice in the two race weekends where his performance was unhampered by grid penalties – Lawson was forced to take a grid drop at Monza as his car needed a raft of new PU components, which understandably hindered his race performance.

Having finished seventh and sixth in Zandvoort and Madrid, he has added to the team’s points tally, and has also been respectable in terms of pace difference to Verstappen. Jumping into the car at a Sprint weekend, while also having to drive the RB22 at a new track, also meant the timing was less than ideal for the New Zealander.

But a year and a half’s worth of added experience seems to have very much paid off this time around.

“I think he has continued to grow as a driver and he's very calm in the car, he is very focused,” added Mekies. “He's certainly making - I don't know if he makes an effort or not - but he's certainly managed to keep things simple in the way he interacts with the team and in the way he tackles his own performance and the car performance.

“So, he's focused on the essentials. He tries to get the basic rights and it's working for him, of course with more time in the car, you can then get to another degree of finesse, maybe. But I think that approach is very, very strong.”

Whether Lawson gets a fourth go at Red Bull remains to be seen, with Hadjar still recovering from the wrist injury he sustained in the summer break.

title: Why Haas see the positives after Madrid disappointment
excerpt:
Esteban Ocon was left "disappointed" after just missing out on points with his 11th-placed finish at the Spanish Grand Prix, the closest he has come to scoring since Monaco.

However, the American squad took the silver linings from their disappointment given their latest raft of upgrades are seemingly delivering. The team’s last big package of parts was all the way back in Canada, and did not have the desired effect as a strong start to the season petered out into plenty of Q1 exits and fighting with the likes of Williams and Aston Martin.

But Haas brought updates to Ollie Bearman’s car in Zandvoort, with Ocon getting the aero package in Monza. There, the track characteristics negated some of the advantage, but it was on full display at the Madring.

“We are all disappointed, I think we could have got much more, we deserved to be in the points today,” Ocon said after the race. “The plan was to get both Audis at the start and we managed to do so, we got both of them off the line and between Turn 1 and 2. I got Gabi [Bortoleto] first off the launch and then Nico [Hulkenberg] around Turn 2. So, that was very good.

“We knew it would be hard to hold them off. But we were in front until the stop, at the stop we lost the position. We need to see what I could have done better, if I could have stopped a little bit better position or what happened as I think it was a decent stop so they must have done a really, really good one.

“But we gave it our all out there. I am proud of everyone, because we come from a long [run] where we were out in Q1, below P15. Now we are fighting for points, so it is pretty positive and encouraging for the rest of the races.”

Ocon qualified 13th in Madrid with his best one-lap performance since Japan. That put him right in the fight with the two Audi cars, although Hulkenberg was able to jump back ahead in the pit stop period when both came in under the VSC.

Audi are the team chasing Haas in the Constructors’ Championship, with the American outfit just four points ahead now thanks to Hulkenberg’s P10 in Madrid. But although their advantage was reduced, Ocon was still confident of the progress Haas have made.

“Since we got the update obviously, we are seeing when the car is healthy and we don’t have the inconsistency we can perform to a decent level and this is what we need to keep doing," he added.

Team boss Ayao Komatsu agreed with his driver, calling it a “really good” sign that they are all so disappointed with P11, a position that looked unthinkable before the summer break.

“The car was functioning very well, the drivers drove well, trackside and remote operations were really good, I think we did our best today. We lost out on the pit stop against Audi, but I don’t believe it was our team’s fault, it’s really the equipment that we need to improve to give them a better chance,” he explained.

“I’m honestly very happy, it was a huge team effort all around, and the car’s consistency was there, no issues as we’ve had previously.”

Even Bearman was able to find some positives, despite running down the order after a pit lane start ti finish 16th. He opted to take on some new power unit components after failing to take part in Qualifying following his heavy FP3 crash on Saturday.

“The car was strong, whenever I had clean air, I was right on pace with our competition. It was just unfortunately very rare that I had that, I was stuck in traffic,” he added.

“I’m positive again, we needed a clean day after what happened yesterday. In that sense we have had that so we can turn the page, learn as much as we can from yesterday, but turn the page, reset and come back stronger in Baku.”

title: Spanish GP 'probably my best race weekend' – Colapinto
excerpt:
Franco Colapinto believes that his seventh-place finish in last weekend's Spanish Grand Prix culminated in "probably my best race weekend" for Alpine this season.

The Argentinian finished best of the rest behind the leading teams on Formula 1's first visit to the Madring after a strong weekend overall.

Colapinto out-qualified Alpine team mate Pierre Gasly for only the second time this season in P9.

Having jumped ahead of Oscar Piastri's McLaren at the start and benefitted when Lewis Hamilton retired his Ferrari, a pit stop under the race's only Virtual Safety Car ensured Colapinto remained in the points at the chequered flag.

"It's probably my best race weekend in terms of execution this year, I maximised everything in Qualifying and did what I had to do today," said Colapinto.

"We will all debrief as a team and continue to develop the car and maximise our performances each weekend.”

The result means Colapinto has finished in the points in back-to-back races, having run as high as third at the previous round in Italy before a small mistake dropped him down the order.

It was also Colapinto's eighth finish inside the points from 14 races, his strong season ultimately convincing Alpine's senior management to re-sign him ahead of the Italian GP weekend.

"I think the team did an amazing job and I maximised everything today and yesterday, so very proud of the result. Very excited for the future," added Colapinto on his performance in Spain.

"It's going well. I think we can take it forward into Baku and the rest of the year."

When asked if anything in particular had clicked this season which had improved his performances, Colapinto replied: "No, I'm just feeling one with the car, I think I'm learning and improving."

title: Audi junior Freddie Slater to race in F2 in 2027
excerpt:
Formula 3 runner-up Freddie Slater, who is part of the Audi Driver Development Programme, will make the step up to Formula 2 with Invicta Racing for the 2027 campaign.

After a standout rookie season that included one Feature Race victory, three pole positions and eight podiums, Slater narrowly lost out on claiming this year’s F3 title by 14 points to Ugo Ugochukwu.

Having signed as the first member of the Audi Driver Development Programme earlier this year, the 18-year-old will move into F2 with Invicta Racing, the squad that won back-to-back Drivers’ and Teams’ Championships in 2024 and 2025.

He will continue to receive support from Audi through his rapid progression in single-seaters, which previously saw Slater impress in the Ginetta Junior Championship, Italian and UAE Formula 4, and the Formula Regional European Championship.

Allan McNish, Director of the Audi Driver Development Programme said: “The move to Formula 2 is the natural next step for Freddie, and an important new phase of his development as a driver.

“He enjoyed a strong Formula 3 season, fighting for the title until the final round – showing his speed, racecraft and progress throughout the year. We are very proud of what Freddie has achieved this season and how he has developed along the way.

“Invicta Racing has had an excellent record in recent years, and we are delighted to be working with them. We believe it is the ideal environment for him, and we look forward to supporting him as he takes on this new challenge in 2027.”

“I’m really excited to be stepping up to Formula 2 with Invicta Racing next year,” Slater added. “I learned a lot in Formula 3 this season, and I feel I have developed as a driver and as a person over the course of the year.

“Invicta has a great record in Formula 2, and I cannot wait to get started with the team and prepare for our campaign together.

“I am also very grateful for the continued support from the Audi Driver Development Programme. There is still a lot for me to learn, and I’m really looking forward to taking on this new challenge.”

title: What we learned from F1's first visit to the Madring
excerpt:
The addition of a new circuit brings with it adrenaline, curiosity and a sense of trepidation as no one quite knows how its debut will play out – and the Madring certainly delivered on all of the above. Here are the biggest lessons we’ve taken away from the Spanish Grand Prix weekend…

How the drivers tackled a new challenge

There are so many factors that can influence the success of a driver’s race, from unpredictable changes in the weather to split-second strategy calls, but for most of the season, they can at least rely on the consistency of track layouts they’ve learned by heart over the years.

They spend time in the simulator until making a corner comes down to muscle memory, and while they were all able to use the same method of preparation for the Madring, nothing compares to racing around it in real life.

The feel of the freshly laid surface, testing just how close to the walls they could get, taking in the indescribable energy of the Spanish capital… they were only able to experience all of this fully when FP1 began on Friday afternoon.

Home favourite Fernando Alonso called it “very technical” and “attractive”, while some drew comparisons to Jeddah’s high speeds and narrow sections. Like the Saudi Arabian track, the Madring quickly showed its bite, with Arvid Lindblad, Lewis Hamilton and Ollie Bearman all caught out in Free Practice.

Once everyone found the initial limits, they began to push them further and further and the lap times didn’t lie, plummeting by over 2s between FP1 and Lando Norris’ magnificent final effort in Qualifying.

Tyre management was king

It’s well documented that the better a driver can manage the tyres, the more likely they are to do well in a race. Extending a stint opens up greater strategic options, while limiting degradation ensures more grip and, consequently, better stability on track.

Of course, that’s easier said than done, as many discovered at the Madring. George Russell explained after Qualifying that “as the track has got faster, I’ve been struggling to get the most out of the tyres”, which he thought was why he couldn’t fight for pole position and wound up sixth in the session.

Moving onto the the Grand Prix, Nico Hulkenberg scored for just the third time this season as Audi continue to close the gap to other midfield teams like Racing Bulls and Alpine, with the German identifying that “managing the tyres and making sure you get to the end” made the difference on a day when the three squads showed “identical pace”.

All the key moments from the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix

Someone else who seemed to thrive in the tyre department – at least until a poorly timed Virtual Safety Car unravelled his race – was McLaren’s Norris, who admitted that he was proud of his performance despite missing out on victory.

He said: “The way I drive, the way I can look after the tyres and get lap time out of it, it's giving me a lot of opportunities and I can do a better job than the others.”

La Monumental lived up to its name

Speaking of tyre management, few corners are as punishing on the Pirelli rubber as La Monumental, which – look away now if you hate puns – was undoubtedly a monumental feature of the circuit.

Standing at 550m long, flanked by up to 45,000 passionate fans, and with a banking gradient of up to 24%, this arena-style section was a treat to watch as drivers accelerated through – even if some weren’t particularly happy with the traffic.

The variety of racing lines caused tempers to flare, especially as La Monumental led to a thrilling blind crest, making the courage required to send it around there even more admirable.

Another twist in the title fight

It’s not often that you hear an F1 driver – some of the most ambitious, ruthless athletes in the world – concede that one of their biggest rivals deserved victory more than them, but that’s exactly what happened in Madrid.

Kimi Antonelli clinched his eighth win of the season to extend his advantage in the Drivers’ Championship to a colossal 81 points, and although he celebrated, he also said: “It’s good to win, but it doesn’t feel as good because I think Lando today deserved to win. But overall, you know, we’ll take it.”

It wasn’t exactly a fair review of his performance, which saw the 20-year-old start in second place before he got ahead of Norris during the pit stops. He then inherited the lead from Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc, who gambled on a long opening stint before finally changing his tyres with fewer than 10 laps to go.

Was there any way for Norris to win in Madrid after the VSC?

Like most races, it was far from straightforward and Antonelli had to resist challenges from both Norris and Max Verstappen in order to reap the reward of his most comfortable position so far in the standings.

Perhaps the biggest revelation came from his team mate Russell, who shared his belief that he’s no longer “in the fight for the drivers’ title” after taking P5 at the Madring. Mercedes boss Toto Wolff didn’t quite agree, emphasising that anything could happen over the remaining rounds, and what looks like “a nice buffer” can rapidly shrink after a couple of crashes or retirements.

With Norris on a fantastic run of form, Ferrari consistently sticking close by, and Russell enjoying minimal pressure on his shoulders, the battle to be crowned the 2026 champion still rages on.

title: 8 moments you might have missed at the Spanish Grand Prix
excerpt:
Another race weekend and another masterclass from Kimi Antonelli, who won the Spanish Grand Prix in its first edition at the Madring.

An element of luck in the Virtual Safety Car timing allowed the Mercedes driver to move past McLaren’s Lando Norris, while a pit stop under the VSC also benefited Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who finished second behind the Italian youngster.

It was a solid race for Charles Leclerc of Ferrari, finishing fourth after leading the race for more than 30 laps, but home hero Carlos Sainz had to retire his Williams, while another Spaniard, Fernando Alonso of Aston Martin, finished only in 17th place.

However, the weekend in Spain’s capital has been equally full of action off track – here are some of the moments you might have missed.

Driving around Madrid in style

Madrid is hosting Formula 1 for the first time in more than four decades.

And Red Bull wanted to let the entire town know that Formula 1 was in town over the weekend, putting the 2012 World Championship-winning car RB8 back on track...quite literally.

The car was driven through Madrid’s rail tunnels on specially designed wheels as part of the On Rails project that began in the city six months ago. It will definitely be one of the enduring images of the maiden Grand Prix at the Madring.

A new look for Williams

A special Grand Prix required a special look – and Williams harked back to an old look, with a new livery and race suits inspired by their championship-winning car FW07C, which raced at Jarama, Madrid, in 1981.

The 1981 season saw a memorable performance from Williams, with the outfit taking home the Teams' honours with drivers Carlos Reutemann and Alan Jones taking second and third in the Drivers' Championship.

Whilst the 2026 running of the Spanish Grand Prix didn't go their way, it was still a future inspired by a great past.

Football enters the paddock…

It’s not possible to avoid the football world when in Madrid. Both past and current players made sure to leave their mark in the paddock over the weekend.

Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto of Alpine had a special chauffeur around Madrid – former Real Madrid player and manager, French legend Zinedine Zidane.

And former Spain internationals enjoyed some padel fun at Madring. Iker Casillas, Fernando Llorente and Raul Gonzalez joined Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton of Ferrari for a few rallies.

After that Hamilton and Leclerc also headed to the Santiago Bernabeu Stadium, home of Real Madrid, to show off some football skills.

Max Verstappen's paddock souvenir came courtesy of Atletico Madrid pair David Hancko and Jan Oblak, as the four-time World Champion scored one of their famed red-and-white stripped jerseys. Madrid was certainly the perfect place for a football-F1 crossover.

Goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois, midfielder Jude Bellingham, defender Trent Alexander-Arnold and forward Vinicius Jr were among those trading the Bernabéu for the Spanish Grand Prix paddock.

Accustomed to performing in front of packed stadiums, the football stars looked right at home, soaking up the atmosphere and joining the crowds eager to witness history as Formula 1 returned to the Spanish capital.

Spanish tennis royalty in the house

It wasn’t just football stars making their way through the paddock. With Formula 1 returning to Madrid for a landmark weekend, 22-time Grand Slam champion Rafael Nadal was never likely to miss the chance to witness a moment of sporting history in his home country.

The Spanish tennis legend was spotted at the circuit alongside his father, Sebastián Nadal, taking in the atmosphere as fans packed the venue for the long-awaited return of Grand Prix racing to the capital.

New chefs in the house!

Can you really spend time in Spain and not try to cook a tortilla? Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas had their own culinary moment in Madrid.

“Cheltteri” took on one of Spain’s most iconic culinary challenges: the tortilla flip. While it might look simple, flipping a Spanish tortilla without turning it into a scrambled mess requires plenty of confidence, technique and a steady hand.

Judging by their efforts, the pair had clearly been paying attention, showing off some impressive skills as they embraced the local culture away from the track. After a weekend in Spain, it seems they’ve become just as adept at flipping tortillas as they are at handling their Cadillac F1 machinery.

Special helmets for the Madring debut

As the Madring made its debut in Formula 1, several drivers wanted to mark the occasion with a custom-designed helmet for the weekend.

Alonso turned heads before a wheel had even been turned thanks to a special all-black helmet created by BOSS. A showcase of style meets speed, the helmet made for a bold fashion-forward statement from the two-time champ.

Sainz marked his home race with a helmet that was as much a tribute to his journey as it was to Spain itself. Wrapped in the colours of the Spanish flag, the special design celebrated the occasion of racing in Madrid while also looking back at the milestones that shaped his career.

References to his very first kart race in 2005 were woven into the artwork, alongside nods to the achievements of his father, two-time World Rally Champion Carlos Sainz Sr.

Norris took a different approach to his Madrid special helmet, collaborating with local artist Sandra Del Pilar and inviting her to "represent the city through her eyes".

The finished design was a striking mix of vivid colours and artistic flourishes inspired by Madrid's character, turning the McLaren driver's helmet into a colourful masterpiece.

An alpine skier with an Alpine driver?

Pierre Gasly found himself in good company in Madrid as he met Olympic and World Champion skier Bode Miller. The pair traded stories from their respective sports, comparing the thrill of carving through snow with the challenge of threading an F1 car through a high-speed corner.

While skis and race cars might seem worlds apart, it made for a fitting meeting between two competitors who have built careers on speed.

title: Toto Wolff reveals Max Verstappen need for 2027 F1 title tilt
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has formed a good relationship with Max Verstappen since entering F1, but could the pair fight for the title next season?

Toto Wolff has revealed what he believes Max Verstappen needs to be able to fight for the championship next season, likely against Kimi Antonelli.

Verstappen sits sixth in the drivers' standings on 145 points after 14 rounds of the 2026 campaign, some 147 points adrift of Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli at the top.

Red Bull, meanwhile, has slipped to fourth in the constructors' championship on 230 points, well behind a dominant Mercedes outfit that leads on 503.

Asked by OE24 whether Red Bull could get back on track for 2027 and set up a title fight between Verstappen and Antonelli, the Mercedes team principal was careful not to write off the four-time champion, while stressing that machinery, not just talent, decides championships.

"Max is the most exceptional driver of this generation, but he also needs the car and the engine to compete for a world championship," Wolff said.

"He has to be the best driver in the best car with the best engine."

Toto Wolff stresses against Kimi Antonelli comparisons

Antonelli has won eight races in 2026, including a breakthrough triumph in China, a title-leading victory in Japan and an emotional home win at Monza after starting 19th following an engine penalty.

Wolff's message, for now, is to let the numbers speak for themselves without forcing the comparison to Verstappen.

Wolff was also asked whether Antonelli, now the championship leader in only his second F1 season, was approaching Verstappen's level as a driver. The Austrian was reluctant to draw any parallel between the two.

"You can't compare a four-time world champion with a rookie in his second Formula 1 year who has only won a little over a handful of races," Wolff said.

"Besides, you shouldn't put too much pressure on Kimi. On the other hand, you can't overstate what he's achieved so far."

title: Madring handed stark money warning after F1 slating
excerpt:
The Madring has received much criticism following its first time hosting the Spanish Grand Prix, with the F1 paddock demanding changes for 2027.

Karun Chandhok has warned that the Madring circuit will need significant further investment if organisers are serious about fixing the lack of overtaking that defined Formula 1's inaugural visit to the track.

The Madring hosted the Spanish Grand Prix for the first time last weekend, with Kimi Antonelli converting second on the grid into victory ahead of Max Verstappen and Lando Norris. But the race itself drew fierce criticism from the paddock over a lack of meaningful action through the field.

Norris was among the most vocal, taking aim at the combination of steering and braking required through Turns 18 and 19. The McLaren driver suggested scrapping the sequence entirely in favour of a longer straight into a wider hairpin.

Haas' Oliver Bearman pointed to the curved braking zones removing any chance of switching lines to dive down the inside, while Gabriel Bortoleto summed up his afternoon behind the wheel by admitting he almost fell asleep.

Verstappen also criticised the track design, saying braking zones that force drivers to steer and brake simultaneously make overtaking essentially impossible.

Chandhok drew a comparison with Monaco, a track that escapes criticism over its lack of passing largely because of its heritage, something Madring cannot claim after just one event.

"The Madring felt like an opportunity lost…. Monaco can get away with being a race with no overtaking because of the history. It looked almost as impossible to pass in Madrid, but just at higher speed," Chandhok wrote on X.

"It won't be easy to tweak an existing track, especially a street one but hope they make some changes for next year."

"The cost and effort in that big 'La Monumental' corner alone must have been huge but sadly they will need to invest more now to improve the 'raceability' around the rest of the track."

Grand Prix

Spanish GP

What Madring needs to become a driver favourite

Madring holds a 10-year contract so will be a regular feature on the F1 calendar, creating plenty of opportunity for change.

Chandhok used Azerbaijan's Baku City Circuit as an example of a layout that improved once its passing zones were understood, despite a similarly underwhelming debut.

"Curved braking areas just don't work for overtaking," added Chandhok. "For example, the first race in Baku in 2016 was utterly dull but nearly every one since then has been good."

"But we knew even after 2016 that the potential was good as they have at least 2 good passing spots on the track, wide entries and straight line braking zone so you can go off line and still stop. That's all any track needs."

title: Kimi Antonelli closing in on F1 history as rivals start to run out of road
excerpt:
It seems it is a case of when, not if, Kimi Antonelli becomes F1 champion.

15 September 2:50PM

Kimi Antonelli is fast closing in on becoming F1's youngest world champion, with the gap behind him growing so wide that his rivals are talking in terms of hope rather than plan.

The Mercedes driver leads the standings on 292 points after Sunday's Spanish Grand Prix victory at the new Madring, 81 clear of team-mate George Russell. As for the rest, Lewis Hamilton is 101 points adrift, Lando Norris 106, and Charles Leclerc 125. Even Max Verstappen, on the podium four times in the last five races, is 147 points behind.

Set against Sebastian Vettel's long-standing record of becoming champion at 23 years and 133 days in 2010, Antonelli, born in August 2006, would smash that mark by well over three years if he seals the title this season.

Whether it's eight or nine rounds remaining, depending on whether an end-of-season race in Europe replaces the Qatar and Abu Dhabi curtain-closing double-header, the 20-year-old simply needs to keep collecting points to take the title.

[Article continues below]

The Antonelli method

What has stood out through his title surge, according to those around him, is a refusal to change approach even as the finish line nears. Antonelli has been explicit that he wants to keep racing the same way he did when the season began.

"There's a long way to go, and I don't really want to drive thinking about the championship," he said. "The thing I want to avoid is driving, going on track for free practice or qualifying or even a race, thinking about or worrying about the championship. That's the thing I want to avoid at all costs."

He repeated the point after the race in Madrid, rejecting any suggestion of switching into a conservative, points-protection mode to nurse his advantage home.

"That's exactly what I don't want to do," he remarked. "I want to keep pushing race by race, keep delivering and keep enjoying it all the way and try to do my best every race and we will see where we end up at the end of the year."

Team principal Toto Wolff has pointed to that mentality as central to the Italian's rise, crediting Mercedes' decision to shield him from external media hype and suggesting his youth, counterintuitively, helps him compartmentalise the pressure rather than buckle under it.

But not every voice has been so convinced. Former champion Jacques Villeneuve warned in May that the real test was still to come.

"So, how will he react when one thing goes wrong? That will be the key thing," said the 1997 F1 title-winner.

Antonelli's own answer points to lessons learned the hard way last year.

"I try to embrace the pressure as much as possible, because I don't want to let the pressure destroy me like it did last year in the European season," he said.

© XPBimages

What the chasers need

For the drivers behind him, the mathematics are turning brutal. Russell, the closest challenger, has already conceded the campaign is slipping away, pointing to a gap built on both pace and misfortune.

"I'm not trying to be delusional, the reality is my team mate has done a better job than me this year," he said. "[I've] Had some bad luck, but he deserves to be leading, and right now he deserves to be in the position he is.

"From my side, I'm just going race by race, going to try and win as many as possible. If I want to win this championship, I'm going to need some luck."

Wolff has not written off his second driver, framing Russell's rough patch as one the strongest competitors recover from.

"We need to find out what it is for him to be able to unleash that potential," said Wolff. "And, of course, there's the psychological side... If you have a run like him this year, you're taking a beating, but the great ones, they recover, and I think that George has all he needs to fight for championships."

That kind of recovery would still leave Russell needing Antonelli to stumble significantly. Wolff himself has flagged the scenario that could realistically reopen the fight: back-to-back retirements for the championship leader, of the sort that struck Hamilton in Madrid. Hamilton's own deficit is arguably already beyond reach, especially after his retirement in Spain.

Norris and Leclerc face a similar reality, both needing sustained Mercedes trouble as much as their own good form to stay relevant to the outcome.

Verstappen's run of podiums has been eye-catching, but a 147-point gap with a maximum of 233 still to play for - should there be nine grands prix - leaves the four-time champion needing something close to a perfect run, allied to Antonelli faltering completely.

None of that is inconceivable, but barring the kind of mechanical misfortune Wolff has already flagged as the one real threat to his young driver, Antonelli's title is now a matter of when, not if.

"Of course, yes, I have a big lead, but you never know what can happen," Antonelli said. "I just need to be ready for anything and keep maximising every opportunity I get, and then we'll see where we end up at the end of the year."

title: Arvid Lindblad passes crucial test as date with driving destiny awaits
excerpt:
Arvid Lindblad has passed his UK driving theory test, the Racing Bulls driver has revealed on Instagram.

The 19-year-old scored 46 out of 50 in the multiple-choice section, comfortably clearing the pass mark of 43. In the hazard perception element, Lindblad recorded 52 out of 75, above the required threshold of 44.

Both sections of the UK theory test are taken in the same sitting, and candidates must clear the pass mark in each to receive an overall pass.

Lindblad's certificate now gives him the green light to book his practical test, which covers an eyesight check, vehicle safety questions, general driving ability, reversing manoeuvres and a period of independent driving.

Under UK rules, a passed theory test remains valid for two years, meaning Lindblad has that window to sit and pass his practical before having to retake the theory exam.

The milestone comes as Lindblad continues his impressive rookie Formula 1 campaign with Red Bull's sister team, following yet another points finish in the Spanish Grand Prix.

Lindblad has 31 points to his name so far this season, with Racing Bulls sitting fifth in the constructors' standings on 77 points after the Madring.

Lindblad's rise through the junior categories saw him graduate to F1 this year as one of the grid's youngest drivers, and his theory pass adds a routine, road-going milestone to a season that has otherwise been about circuits rather than the Highway Code.

Attention now turns to the practical test, and to Baku, where Lindblad and F1 head next for round 15 of the championship on 24 September.

title: Legendary Ayrton Senna F1 car set for 'extra mile' revival
excerpt:
One of F1's most recognisable cars is set for a major revival, with 10 full-scale replicas of the iconic Lotus 97T to be built.

Memento Exclusives has confirmed that the mystery heritage project it teased earlier this year centres on the Lotus 97T, the car driven by Elio De Angelis and Ayrton Senna in the 1985 Formula 1 season.

Only 10 full-scale replicas of the car will ever be built, produced in partnership with Classic Team Lotus.

Memento Exclusives is best known as the show car supplier to F1 and as operator of the officially licensed platform F1 Authentics, having produced replicas of current-generation cars for teams on the grid since 2019.

Those creations regularly appear at livery launches, exhibitions, circuits and partner activations worldwide, with small numbers made available to private collectors.

The 97T project marks the first heritage edition the company has produced, a different challenge to replicating a modern car built from CAD data.

Classic Team Lotus has provided archive material never previously shared for this purpose, including hand-drawn designs, original build documents and heritage reference data.

The show car will be built using many of the same materials and construction techniques as the 1985 original, with input from people who worked on that car. Each of the 10 will carry an individual chassis plate, formally registering it within the Team Lotus archive.

Classic Lotus set for 'forever' revival with exciting project

The 97T carried Team Lotus back to winning form three years after Colin Chapman's death, with Gérard Ducarouge arriving as technical director and the John Player black-and-gold livery retained.

De Angelis, the team's most prolific driver by grand prix starts, was partnered by a young Senna for 1985.

Senna won from pole in torrential conditions at the Portuguese Grand Prix by more than a minute, De Angelis followed up with victory at Imola, and Senna added a third win in Belgium. The car took seven pole positions across the 16-race season.

Classic Team Lotus, based at the original team factory in Hethel, Norfolk, now handles licensing along with the restoration, maintenance and operation of historic Team Lotus cars.

Clive Chapman, managing director of Classic Team Lotus, said: "The interest, excitement and emotion the Lotus 97T generates is extraordinary. To have it captured forever is exactly what we like to do at Classic Team Lotus, to preserve and to celebrate."

"That is what this project is going to do. Memento Exclusives is going the extra mile to make something that is really special. We have been impressed with their attention to detail and commitment to make a car of the highest standard and accuracy."

"I am confident the end result is going to be something we are happy with, that they are proud of and that people will enjoy."

title: How Lewis Hamilton title chances went completely up in smoke
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton's world championship challenge has unravelled in spectacular fashion since Silverstone, with the seven-time champion falling from 32 points behind Kimi Antonelli to a near-insurmountable 101-point deficit in the space of six races.

The slide has been relentless. Hamilton trailed the Mercedes driver by 32 points after the British Grand Prix, where he finished third behind Charles Leclerc and George Russell.

That gap grew to 45 points in Belgium, 50 in Hungary, 59 in the Netherlands and 76 in Italy, before a retirement in Madrid blew it out to 101.

Reliability has played its part. Hamilton's Spanish Grand Prix ended after just seven laps when his SF-26 suffered a brake problem, with the pedal stepping and going long under braking, forcing him to clip a wall before being unable to stop the car.

Ferrari has launched a formal investigation into the fault, though team principal Fred Vasseur said the exact cause remained unclear at the time.

But reliability alone does not explain a 101-point swing. Antonelli has simply been faster and more consistent, winning in Belgium, Italy and Spain, while Hamilton has been unable to match the raw pace of the Mercedes or, at times, his own team-mate.

Ferrari power unit disadvantage remains constant Lewis Hamilton struggle

The most uncomfortable pattern for Hamilton has been Leclerc's emergence as Ferrari's clear reference driver. The Monegasque took victory at Silverstone in a Ferrari one-three, then finished ahead of his team-mate in Belgium, Hungary and again in Spain, where he was fourth to Hamilton's retirement.

Part of that shift traces back to a setup change Leclerc made before the British Grand Prix, adopting an approach closer to Hamilton's own braking configuration to combat high-speed instability he had struggled with earlier in the season.

Ferrari's updates around that race also sharpened the car's aerodynamic balance and straight-line efficiency, benefits Leclerc has appeared to extract more consistently than Hamilton across long stints.

Hamilton, by contrast, has repeatedly described a car that felt unpredictable beneath him. After Zandvoort he said he had lost confidence in the balance through qualifying and the race itself, describing the car as constantly breaking away from him.

Even after a major Barcelona upgrade package in June, which included a new front wing, nose, sidepods, floor and diffuser, Hamilton suggested Ferrari remained a chunk off the pace of McLaren and Mercedes.

The Scuderia has also leaned on the FIA's Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities framework to bring an upgraded power unit through the European season, an avenue Mercedes is reportedly preparing to exploit again for the flyaway rounds, which would pile further pressure on Ferrari's engine programme.

Vasseur has been explicit that Ferrari will not abandon development of the SF-26 despite the widening gap to Mercedes, pointing out that roughly 80 per cent of current mechanical and aerodynamic work carries over to the 2027 car under regulatory continuity. That is a long-term justification, not a solution to Hamilton's immediate problem.

Hamilton himself has conceded the mathematics of the title fight are now brutal, calling it the biggest gap he has faced, while insisting his focus each weekend has to be on his own performance rather than the widening deficit.

With likely eight rounds remaining after Madrid, that discipline may be all that is left for him to control.

title: Lando Norris opens up on 'complicated subject' after brutal loss
excerpt:
Lando Norris would have won the Spanish Grand Prix at the Madring, had it not been for a virtual safety car. Are changes needed to the rules?

15 September 11:30AM

Lando Norris has called for a change the "complicated subject" that is the virtual safety car regulations after a poorly timed neutralisation cost him victory at the Spanish Grand Prix.

The McLaren driver led from pole at the Madring only for a VSC, triggered when Lance Stroll stopped his Aston Martin at Turn 20 with a brake failure, to hand rivals a near-free pit stop.

Norris had already passed the pit entry when the VSC came out, forcing him to complete a full lap at delta speed while those behind ducked in for a fraction of the usual time loss. He crossed the line third, behind race winner Kimi Antonelli and Max Verstappen.

Asked if changes should be made to the regulations regarding VSCs, Norris explained that it had been raised repeatedly by drivers over the years.

"Yeah, I mean, it's been brought up many times over the years by different drivers," said Norris. "I think there's always probably some cons to doing it, but it's tough.

"Like I said, I've won from it in the past, I've lost from it in the past. Over the course of a season, it's hard to know if it's a good thing or a bad thing. It probably equals out over time. Of course, it just hurts more, the fact that I lose a win.

"You know, there's literally nothing I could do as a driver today to do a better job. Pole, led the race, and to lose it for nothing in my control is, I don't think, how a race should be won. But I think people, I hope people agree, I think people would agree.

"But it is racing and it's happened, so I can't really complain about it. I can be upset about it, but I can't really complain about it."

Lando Norris hopeful future VSC pain can be avoided

Norris went on to outline possible solutions that have circulated in drivers' briefings, including a minimum one-lap VSC period or closing the pit lane entirely during a neutralisation.

The McLaren driver continued: "And I think there are things, because we have spoken about it in the past several times, about how it can be at least covered for one lap or everyone has the opportunity to do the pit stops, or you just block the pit entry and no one can box apart from if you have a puncture or something, you know.

"So, I think there's a few things you could do to make it more simple and more fair for everyone, but that's a bigger discussion. You know, this is not something I can just ask for. I think it's something, as a group of drivers, I think we would all want, but there's a lot more to it.

"You know, depending on if it's raining and there's a VSC and you're on slicks, does it mean you can box or not? You know, so it's a complicated subject. But I think as a collection of drivers, if we all talk about it, I think everyone wants the same thing, and that's just fairness for everyone.

"So yeah, of course I'm complaining about it today. I could benefit from it next week, next time out, and I could win because of it. So yeah, I have to take it on the chin, but I just hope it doesn't happen to anyone again because it's just not how you should lose a race."

title: George Russell makes major Max Verstappen claim

Teammates Closer to Verstappen

George Russell believes the new generation of F1 cars has fundamentally altered the balance of power between team-mates on the grid, singling out Max Verstappen's improved rivals at Red Bull as the clearest example.

Russell, who sits second in the drivers' championship, 81 points behind Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli, says this season has thrown up unusual patterns when comparing team-mate battles to previous years.

"It's been a strange season when you look at the competitiveness of [Oscar] Piastri against Lando [Norris] last year, Charles [Leclerc] compared to Lewis [Hamilton], and even the dominance of Max against all of his team-mates in the previous era," said Russell.

[Article continues below]

Hadjar and Lawson closing the gap

Russell pointed to his own struggles against Antonelli as part of a wider trend among the sport's usual benchmark drivers.

"This year, myself, Charles and Oscar are struggling much more compared to our team-mates," said Russell.

Verstappen has again had two team-mates this season - Isack Hadjar for the first 11 grands prix, and Liam Lawson for the last three after the French driver sustained a wrist injury during the summer break whilst boxing training.

The Dutch driver currently sits sixth in the standings on 145 points, with Hadjar seventh on 71 points and Lawson ninth on 59 points, a gap far smaller than the four-time champion's usual margin over his team-mates in recent seasons.

Russell believes the shift comes down to overlapping driving styles among the current crop of frontrunners.

"We've all got pretty similar driving styles, and the drivers are performing very well this year," he remarked.

"Kimi, Lewis, and Lando have also got quite similar driving styles. So to me, it's pretty clear with this car, with these tyres, what I need to achieve.

"The trends are there, with, as I said, those drivers I just mentioned."

Former Williams F1 junior Zak O'Sullivan will race full-time in Formula E next season after Envision confirmed the British driver as its newest addition to the grid.

The 21-year-old steps up to a race seat having spent the past year embedded within the team, taking on simulator duties alongside a string of rookie outings. O'Sullivan's first taste of the Gen3 Evo came at the Jeddah E-Prix in Season 11, when he made his Formula E bow during the rookie free practice session.

He has since been given further outings, driving in Berlin last year, while appearances in Miami and Madrid came in 2026. He topped the timesheets during the rookie session in Miami.

O'Sullivan arrives with a CV that already carries plenty of silverware. After a string of karting wins, he moved into single-seaters and narrowly missed out on the 2020 British Formula 4 title before claiming the GB3 Championship the following year.

Two seasons in Formula 3 followed, yielding four victories and the runner-up spot in the 2023 standings, before a step up to Formula 2 in 2024 brought wins in Monaco and at Spa-Francorchamps. Due to a lack of funding, he left F2 in September that year.

He has since added Japanese Super Formula to his résumé, broadening a record that already points to speed, adaptability and a habit of winning across categories.

"We are very happy to announce Zak as a full-time driver for Season 13 and beyond," said Envision team boss Sylvain Filippi.

"We’ve spent a lot of time with him during Season 12, and he has established himself in the team very well.

"We have been very impressed with Zak’s performance, both on the track during the rookie sessions, and his commitment off-track. We are very much looking forward to seeing him race in our car and embarking on his rookie season in Formula E with us."

Zak O'Sullivan eager to put Formula E learnings into practice

The announcement of O'Sullivan's promotion to a race seat falls exactly 24 hours after Envision confirmed the signing of Maximilian Günther.

It represents an entirely new pairing for the team for the start of the Gen4 era, with O'Sullivan eager to put what he learnt on the sidelines into practice.

"I am very excited to be joining the team full-time for the upcoming season," O'Sullivan said.

"I've spent the last year embedding myself into the team and can't wait to get the season started in the new Gen4 car.

"Formula E is a championship I've had my sights set on for a long time, so to be joining the grid for Season 13 at such an exciting time for the sport is a great feeling."

title: Madring set for 2027 overhaul after drivers savage overtaking woes
excerpt:
If changes are made, then it could become a thoroughly entertaining circuit, for the grand prix on Sunday, not just for qualifying on Saturday.

Spanish Grand Prix organisers are preparing to redesign three sections of its under-fire Madring circuit for 2027 following a dire inaugural race.

Whilst the 22-corner track situated in the north-east of the Spanish capital Madrid delivered a superb qualifying spectacle, the race itself drew fierce criticism from many associated with F1 over a near-total absence of meaningful passing, with several corners identified as fundamentally flawed for wheel-to-wheel racing.

It is understood that following the first lap and the usual plethora of positional changes, there were just four notable overtakes. In contrast, there were 10 at this year's Monaco Grand Prix.

Four-time F1 champion Max Verstappen was blunt in his assessment of the layout's core problem, criticising braking zones that force drivers to turn and slow simultaneously.

"For the braking zones, they need to learn that it should never be that you have to steer and combine that under braking," said Verstappen. "It doesn't allow any kind of overtaking. So, in terms of track design, I think it can be better."

Reigning champion Lande Norris went further, questioning the entire concept behind the circuit's design.

"I don't know how someone looks at this design and goes 'mint'," remarked the McLaren driver. "The fact you have to turn and brake basically defeats the whole object of racing. They can do some simple changes."

Grand Prix

Spanish GP

Madring's trio of problem zones

The Turn 5/6 chicane, reached after a long run along the Ribera del Sena, was singled out as the most damaging section. Its curved braking zone and narrow entry stripped drivers of alternative lines, making side-by-side racing there almost impossible without heavy risk of contact.

Antonelli described a near-miss with Norris through that exact sequence.

"It definitely doesn't create overtaking opportunities and it doesn't push you to try and make a move, because 80 percent of the time you might have contact," said Mercedes' championship leader.

Referring to an opening-lap incident, he added: "I think especially in the second chicane, if I would have turned in there, me and Lando would have touched and probably gone into the wall."

Haas driver Oliver Bearman echoed the complaint, pointing to the same curved-braking problem as a fundamental design flaw.

"That kind of curved braking takes away any possibility of different lines and sending one up the inside," he said. "So that's a shame and maybe a bit of an oversight."

Turn 13, arriving straight after the banked La Monumental curve, is a second target. Despite the slipstream built up through the banking, the corner's medium-speed profile does not offer a heavy enough braking zone to convert that tow into a genuine passing chance.

The technical, low-speed sequence through Turns 18 and 19 ahead of the final complex was also flagged as a bottleneck that kills momentum rather than feeding a straight into a hairpin.

Madring event managing director Luis Garcia Abad confirmed the FIA has already outlined a path forward.

"Being honest with you, the FIA defined clearly which is the way to improve the track layout, and we will be open because we will have to reinstall the track for next year," he said.

© XPBimages

Ferrari and Mercedes bosses strike a more balanced tone

Not every voice in the paddock was as critical of the weekend as a whole. Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur praised the event's staging even while acknowledging the racing itself needs work.

"For me, overall, the event was mega," said Vasseur, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365.

"The infrastructure, we were mega welcome in the city. We have also to be fair with them and to congratulate Madrid for the job done on this side."

Confirming that initial talks followed, he added: "They [the organisers] came to us on Thursday, but it was very early, and then on Friday evening to see if we think that it would be difficult to overtake.

"They are keen to do modifications in the future. They probably have more latitude in Madrid than in Monaco to change something.

"So let's work together to see if we can do something better. But overall, we have to be fair with them. It was a good event."

Mercedes boss Toto Wolff struck a similar note, framing the circuit's debut as a promising foundation that now needs refining.

"For a first [event], it's probably one of the best, or maybe the best I've seen so far," said Wolff, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365.

"It's a temporary circuit. [But] They've built something that is challenging for the drivers, a mini Macau or a mini Monaco, and the location is good.

"We're thinking about how much more can we do next year in terms of the events here or presentations because we have the space and that's very rare.

"That is the tricky bit. Doing a track that is spectacular, also for the drivers, and then building it in a way that there is lots of overtaking.

"I had a discussion with the CEO of the circuit and they are totally open-minded about next year. They said they've had discussions with the FIA - 'What is it we should do? How should we lay the track out when it comes to overtaking?'

"There is a constant discussion and I think that they are on it and understand that we can tweak it a little bit here or there."

Norris, for his part, made clear he expects the promised changes to materialise before Madring returns to the calendar.

"They can do some simple changes," he said. "I hope they do it because then it should be more exciting for everyone."

title: Sebastian Vettel 'blown away' as major motorsport event reveals fresh location
excerpt:
Fresh details have been released about the 2027 Race of Champions, one of the most exciting annual motorsport events featuring some of the biggest names.

The 2027 Race of Champions will be held in New Zealand for the first time in its history, with Wellington's Hnry Stadium set to host the event across January 9-10. Sebastian Vettel is returning again, and was "blown away" by the country's beauty.

The stadium, formerly known as Westpac Stadium and colloquially referred to as the "Cake Tin", will have its natural grass pitch transformed into a temporary asphalt circuit for the occasion.

The venue, which seats approximately 34,500, has never before staged a motorsport event of this scale.

Oceania only entered the Race of Champions calendar in 2025, when Sydney hosted the event for the first time. New Zealand's turn has been secured through the government's Events Attraction Package, with the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) backing the event as part of a push to boost domestic and international visitation.

Four-time Formula 1 world champion Vettel has been confirmed among the headline names for Wellington, returning to the event after his appearance at last year's edition in Sydney.

The German revealed that his own visit to New Zealand ahead of ROC Sydney played a part in the country landing the event.

"Before ROC Sydney I went for a first quick visit to New Zealand and was blown away by the beauty of the country, so I told the organisers jokingly can you pls bring the next ROC to New Zealand," he said.

"I am really looking forward to competing against so many other Champions from across the globe at the Race Of Champions in Wellington in January and get a chance to visit more of New Zealand."

Valtteri Bottas returns once again in off-season boost

Alongside Vettel, Cadillac F1 driver Valtteri Bottas has also been confirmed for Wellington, along with two-time Bathurst 1000 winner Chaz Mostert and rally star Hayden Paddon.

Mostert arrives as the reigning 2025 Supercars champion and was runner-up at ROC Sydney last year, beating both Bottas and Vettel before losing the individual final to Sébastien Loeb.

Paddon brings a rally résumé that includes a World Rally Championship victory at the 2016 Rally Argentina and back-to-back European Rally Championship titles in 2023 and 2024.

Organisers have said further names will be announced in the coming weeks, with the full entry list yet to be finalised.

ROC president Fredrik Johnsson said the event's arrival in New Zealand had been driven by the depth of local talent and enthusiasm for motorsport in the country.

Bottas, who competed at ROC Sydney last year, said he was eager to return to the event during the off-season.

"Race Of Champions is such a special and exciting event and I'm so happy that it's back again," the Finn said.

"I can't wait to compete in Wellington, New Zealand, with all the other drivers from different categories, racing on the same track, in different types of cars, which makes ROC really spectator friendly.

"ROC New Zealand is going to be another exciting race with great atmosphere both for us drivers and the fans. Also personally I feel it's really good to drive something during the off-season and there is no better place to do it than at ROC, so I'm really looking forward to January!"

title: Lando Norris completes rare non-F1 test
excerpt:
Lando Norris has completed a test in McLaren's new hypercar, which is set to join the World Endurance Championship (WEC) next year.

The reigning Formula 1 world champion headed to Portimao following his agonising defeat in the Spanish Grand Prix, where he got to grips with the MCL-HY.

Norris managed 38 laps of the circuit following an acclimatisation run, with his programme having included a number of development items to deliver feedback to the team.

He worked alongside McLaren Racing factory driver Mikkel Jensen, while Laurens Vanthoor, who will join the outfit in 2027, was also present at the track test.

Like Max Verstappen, Norris has not kept it a secret that he has significant interest in making a future appearance in the Le Mans 24 Hours.

Testing McLaren's new hypercar keeps a door to that very much wide open and offers the British team a chance to see what he is capable of.

"First of all, a big thanks to the McLaren Hypercar Team for letting me drive the MCL-HY," said Norris. It was great for them to give me a chance to have a bit of fun and try something new, particularly during their busy preparations for next year.

"I think we also collected some valuable data, and I hope I was able to bring a different set of feelings, comments, and perspectives on things, which is useful for the team in this crucial testing period.

"It was cool for me personally to work with this team, and it was exciting to try new machinery too. I've not done a proper test in anything other than an F1 car for years now, so the fact I got to try something different, especially still as part of the McLaren family, was very special.

"It was a fun day in a quick car on a cool track, helping the team prepare for the start of WEC next year. A big thanks to everyone involved, I can't wait to get back in the car in the future."

Lando Norris makes instant impact in McLaren WEC test

Norris' appearance in Portugal was not his first outing in McLaren's new hypercar, as the F1 driver took it up the iconic Goodwood hill during the summer.

McLaren's hypercar team offered Norris the opportunity following Goodwood, where he showed significant interest at driving it again.

"We are all racers at McLaren Racing, and competing in Formula 1, IndyCar and the World Endurance Championship creates exciting cross-series opportunities," said Ian James, McLaren WEC team principal.

"Lando was keen to drive the MCL-HY beyond his Goodwood Hill run, so we invited him to join our private Portimão test. As we fully expected he adapted very quickly, integrated seamlessly and provided valuable feedback to support the car’s development.

"It was a pleasure to have him with the team, we wish him every success for the rest of the Formula 1 season, and we look forward to welcoming him back into the McLaren Hypercar Team soon."
